name: Stonepath — Pre-Industrial Spiritual Naturalism
description: Stonepath emerged from the convergence of several BCI-refuser and analog-naturalist circles, coalescing around the teachings of a Tier 1 elder known only as Maren Solás, who preaches that human consciousness was ecologically calibrated for a pre-electrified world and that every layer of technology added since represents spiritual debt accumulating interest. Members practice stone-working, fermentation, hand-grinding of grain, and seasonal fasting aligned with pre-Gregorian lunar cycles sourced from a synthesis of Haudenosaunee, Andean, and West African agrarian traditions. Stonepath is distinguished from similar movements by its genuine agricultural presence — they maintain three hidden rooftop growing plots in Tier 1 and one contested green-space on the Shelf's northern edge called the Patience Ground.
cultural_impact: Stonepath's fermentation practices have leaked into Shelf food culture broadly, with their unlicensed grain spirits and preserved vegetables traded widely at ghost markets — this has created a minor but persistent gray-market food economy that operates outside corporate nutrition licensing. Their rejection of BCI makes them valuable to certain criminal organizations as messengers and safe-house keepers who cannot be remotely scanned.
locations: Patience Ground, northern Shelf edge, Tier 1
The Grind, a basement meeting space beneath a decommissioned water processing unit, Tier 1
story_hooks: The Patience Ground is set to be demolished for a corporate logistics hub expansion — Stonepath elders are divided between peaceful resistance and accepting an offer from a Shelf crime faction to defend the land with violence.

A Tier 4 executive's child has joined Stonepath and disappeared into Tier 1; the executive wants them extracted, but the child claims they joined voluntarily and the community's no-BCI policy means there's no digital trail to follow.

Someone has been poisoning Stonepath's fermentation stores with a compound that mimics natural spoilage — the community suspects a corporate food-licensing enforcement arm, but the perpetrator may be closer to home.
